headline: Civil servant WFH: fuel saver, workplace reform, or both?
context: Phased WFH for federal public servants, set out in the 26 March 2026 PMO speech, began 15 April under a PSD circular: 8 km+ commutes, SPOT-Me geolocation, KPIs, frontline services excluded. From 1 Aug 2026 a Hybrid Working Day policy replaced it.

changes.summary: Correction: Added the PSD circular in force from 15 April (8 km commute threshold, SPOT-Me attendance). Wage-bill figures corrected to Budget 2026 estimates: RM109.4 billion in emoluments, RM42.8 billion in retirement charges.

Correction: the PSD circular covered officers with a one-way commute of more than 8 km; earlier editions said within 8 km. Update: from 1 Aug 2026 a Hybrid Working Day policy (three office days, two remote) replaced the West Asia WFH arrangement.

cards.big: WFH for federal public servants was fine-tuned on 26 March, the day fuel quotas were also cut.
cards.sub: The stated trigger is fuel conservation amid the Hormuz crisis. A PSD circular was issued by 2 April; implementation started 15 April.

cards.big: The circular excluded frontline workers by design: nurses, teachers, police. It covered officers in specified locations with a one-way commute of more than 8 km.
cards.sub: The specified locations were Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya, Selangor and the state capitals.

cards.big: Budget 2026 estimates federal emoluments at RM109.4B and retirement charges at RM42.8B. Malaysia had over 1.3 million civil servants in September 2025.
cards.sub: World Bank cautions that cross-country civil-service ratios are difficult to compare. Wage-bill stress is the firmer claim.

cards.big: The UK runs hybrid with attendance targets. Singapore's guidelines set a process for flexible-work requests. Malaysia's 2 April PSD circular set KPIs and SPOT-Me geolocation.
cards.sub: As of early April, Penang had declined state-level WFH and Sarawak had issued no state directive. State alignment was uneven.

cards.big: The question is no longer whether WFH was 'announced with no details'. It is whether the published rules will be enforced and whether output, not attendance, becomes the measure.
Crisis-born reforms can stick if the rules outlast the crisis. The PSD circular is a real document; the test is whether departments measure output and publish results.
